nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics; precision measurement
motivation: Katori proposed the 'magic wavelength' optical lattice, in which neutral atoms are held in a light field that shifts both clock levels equally. This lets many atoms be interrogated at once, free of motion and trap-light perturbations, and he realized the first such clocks. Ye turned the concept into the most precise and accurate frequency standards ever built. He reached uncertainties near 10^-18 and beyond, with ultrastable lasers, many-body control of the lattice and frequency-comb links. These clocks resolve gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, test the constancy of fundamental constants, search for dark matter, and drive the coming redefinition of the SI second. The invention is a wonderful example of clever experimental control over quantum states giving physicists an entirely new instrument. Its influence reaches geodesy, fundamental physics and quantum metrology.
